entities.summary: Henry VII of England, also known as Henry Tudor, was the first monarch of the House of Tudor, seizing the crown on 22 August 1485 until his death in 1509. Born into the Lancastrian faction of the House of York, Henry VII's claim to the throne was supported by the powerful Earl of Richmond, his uncle. He was the son of Edmund Tudor and Margaret Beaufort, making him a descendant of King Henry IV and a great-grandson of King Edward III. Henry VII's marriage to Elizabeth of York, daughter of the defeated House of York, united the rival houses and strengthened his claim to the throne. He implemented a policy of reconciliation with the defeated Yorkists, pardoning many of their leaders and allowing them to return to their lands. This approach earned him the nickname 'the Peacemaker.' Henry VII's reign marked the beginning of a new era of stability and prosperity in England, which would continue until the reign of his son, Henry VIII. The reign of Henry VII is often seen as a turning point in English history, as it brought an end to the Wars of the Roses and established a strong foundation for the Tudor dynasty. The Tudor Rose, a symbol of the union between the houses of Lancaster and York, remains a powerful emblem of English heritage. Henry VII's legacy extends beyond his own reign, as he laid the groundwork for the growth of the English economy and the development of a more centralized state.
